title: ETX5900 S2 2026 quiz bank: adaptation for the ETX1100/ETX5900 eight-week intensive
text:
The source bank has 11 original weeks, usually 20 questions each. S3 Q7 below means Question 7 in source Week 3, not intensive Week 3. It contains marked answers and should remain an instructor source file. Keep means the statistical task is suitable; all retained questions still need answers and solution cues removed before student release. Adapt means retain the skill but replace data, context, or wording. Exclude means omit from the core eight-week quizzes.
The original Elecmart, Hytex, PlanFinan, Health care, Hospital Quality, and Data for quiz 11 workbooks were not found in this project. The embedded tables and image references in the Markdown file do supply some questions without those workbooks. Current intensive workbooks can supply replacement data, but the old numerical answers must be recalculated.
This is an instructor selection review, not a released quiz or answer key. Follow AGENTS.md, course_info.R, and the current weekly slides and workbooks when adapting items. The eight weekly quizzes are individual and together carry 15% of the ETX1100 assessment. Weeks 1–4 provide the scope for the Week 4 written assignment; regression and business modelling begin later. The outcome tags below use the ETX1100 outcomes as planning labels. Confirm the official ETX5900 outcome wording before using them as its formal assessment map.
Current Week 5 decision: teach and assess the chi-square test of independence as a categorical-relationship application of LO4. Quiz 5 may assess hypotheses, expected counts, cell contributions, degrees of freedom, CHISQ.TEST, conditions, and a contextual decision. Quiz 4 and the written assignment remain limited to the material taught through Week 4. The source-bank S6 label is its old week number, not the intensive week.
Excel boundary: the Analysis ToolPak is the only analysis add-in in the current course. Ordinary worksheet formulas and probability functions, PivotTables, charts, filters, and manual scenario comparisons remain appropriate. Where an item requires a fitted regression, align its output and instructions with Data > Data Analysis > Regression. Do not require Solver, Goal Seek, What-If Data Tables, or programming-based optimisation. A ToolPak regression question alone assesses LO5; an LO6 item must also test how the fitted relationship enters a business decision model.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Today’s journey

Select methods from a business question and variable types.
Analyse ETF’s supermarket staffing and profit case.
Turn output into recommendations and limitations.
Correct common statistical misconceptions.
Consolidate the six learning outcomes for the examination.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
The four purposes








Purpose
Core question
Example method




Describe
What happened in this sample?
tables, charts, summaries


Infer
What does the sample suggest about a population?
intervals, tests


Predict
What outcome is expected for given inputs?
regression


Decide
Which listed feasible option performs best?
ToolPak regression plus an Excel formula model

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Watch me: unpack a business question

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Now you try: method selection





Choose a purpose and method for each question:

What percentage of stores open 24 hours?
Is population mean service quality above 80?
Which staffing factors predict profit?
Which listed price gives the highest predicted profit within a capacity limit?
Are loyalty tier and renewal associated in the customer population?

Justify each choice from the variables and claim.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Business context
A supermarket chain is considering incentives intended to improve store performance.
Open week8-case-data.xlsx.
Each row represents a store. Variables cover:

profit and operating context;
manager and crew tenure;
manager and crew skill; and
service quality.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Data dictionary highlights







Variable
Meaning




Profit
current-year store profit


MTenure, CTenure
average manager and crew tenure in months


MgrSkill, CrewSkill
staffing skill measures


ServQual
service-quality score


Pop, Comp, Visibility, PedCount, Res, Hours24
store context



Confirm units and coding in the workbook before analysing.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Watch me: audit before modelling

Check row count, headers, and missing values.
Classify each variable.
Inspect ranges and units.
Create descriptive statistics for key numerical variables.
Plot Profit and ServQual for unusual values.

Document—not silently delete—anything suspicious.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Staffing questions
The ETF case asks:

Are manager and crew skills associated?
Do crews stay longer where managers stay longer?
Are skill measures associated with service quality?
Is service quality associated with profit?

These are observational association questions—not experiments.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Watch me: correlation matrix
Use Data → Data Analysis → Correlation for selected numerical variables.

Include labels.
Confirm the output is symmetric with 1s on the diagonal.
Pair strong correlations with scatterplots.
Describe direction, strength, form, and unusual points.
Avoid ranking variables by correlation alone.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
High service-quality stores
ETF defines excellent service as ServQual >= 90.
Comparing skill across this threshold can be useful descriptively, but dichotomising a numerical variable discards information. Use it to complement—not replace—the continuous analysis.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: compare service groups
text:
Now you try: compare service groups





Create an ExcellentService flag and compare CrewSkill and MgrSkill across groups.
Use appropriate centre, spread, and plots. State what the comparison suggests and why it does not establish that skill caused service quality.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Model service quality
Begin with a focused explanatory question:
ServQual_i=\beta_0+\beta_1MTenure_i+\beta_2CTenure_i+\beta_3MgrSkill_i+\beta_4CrewSkill_i+\varepsilon_i.
The chosen variables should reflect a rationale, not merely every available column.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Watch me: service-quality model

Fit the model in Excel.
Write the fitted equation.
Interpret two partial slopes.
Evaluate adjusted R^2 and Significance F.
Inspect coefficient p-values and residual plots.
Record limitations before considering reduction.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: refine the service model
text:
Now you try: refine the service model





Create one defensible reduced model.
Compare it with the full model using coefficient stability, adjusted R^2, standard error, individual tests, overall evidence, residuals, and interpretability. Recommend one model.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Model profit in context
Profit may depend on staffing and store environment. Candidate predictors include tenure, skills, service quality, population, competition, visibility, pedestrian count, residential context, and 24-hour operation.
Adding controls can change staffing coefficients because store context is not evenly distributed.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Watch me: profit model
Build a full model with a clearly stated rationale.

Identify dummy-variable coding.
Interpret staffing slopes conditionally.
Distinguish statistical from practical significance.
Check overall fit and residuals.
Consider whether correlated predictors make individual coefficients unstable.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Evidence chain
A defensible recommendation connects:
question → data → method → result → limitation → action
Weak reports jump directly from a significant coefficient to a policy. Strong reports explain the comparison, uncertainty, assumptions, feasible action, and what should be tested next.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Watch me: carry a ToolPak model into a decision
text:
Watch me: carry a ToolPak model into a decision
Suppose a pricing pilot covering AUD 50–105 gives the fitted equation
\widehat{Units}=701-5.01\times Price.
Before recommending a price, identify which numbers came from the Analysis ToolPak and which business inputs are still needed. State the observed price range and the production rule you would check.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: compare feasible prices
text:
Now you try: compare feasible prices





Compare listed prices AUD 80, 90, and 100. Assume unit cost AUD 40, fixed cost AUD 1,200, and capacity 340 units.
For each price calculate predicted units, whole units planned after the capacity rule, revenue, cost, and profit. Recommend one listed price and explain one way the recommendation could change if the assumptions are wrong.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Misconception 1: conditional probability
“Because 70% of app users are highly satisfied, 70% of highly satisfied customers use the app.”
The statement reverses the condition:
P(Satisfied\mid App)\ne P(App\mid Satisfied).
The denominators differ.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: correct the conditional claim
text:
Now you try: correct the conditional claim





Rewrite the claim correctly and describe the additional contingency-table information needed to calculate the reversed conditional probability.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Misconception 2: confidence intervals
“There is a 95% probability that this fixed population mean is inside our calculated interval.”
Frequentist confidence attaches 95% to the long-run method, not a probability assigned to the fixed parameter after observing the interval.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: repair the interval statement
text:
Now you try: repair the interval statement





Write a correct contextual interpretation and explain why the interval does not describe where 95% of individual customers lie.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Misconception 3: regression coefficients
“The manager-skill coefficient is the raw difference in profit between high- and low-skill stores.”
In multiple regression it is a conditional comparison, holding other included predictors constant. Its unit and coding must be stated.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: repair the coefficient claim
text:
Now you try: repair the coefficient claim





Choose one coefficient from your profit model and provide:

a correct interpretation;
the base category if relevant; and
one reason it should not be described as causal.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Misconception 4: evidence and importance
“Because p<0.05, the effect is large, useful, and the null hypothesis has a less than 5% chance of being true.”
A p-value addresses compatibility with H_0 under assumptions. Effect size, uncertainty, costs, and practical thresholds require separate evidence.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: repair the evidence claim
text:
Now you try: repair the evidence claim





Rewrite the claim using the estimate, confidence interval, and business threshold. State what decision would follow if the effect is statistically clear but too small to matter.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Learning-outcome map

Classify and visualise data.
Calculate and interpret probability.
Sample, estimate, and test claims.
Analyse relationships.
Build simple and multiple regression in Excel.
Formulate and solve spreadsheet business models.

The examination can ask you to select, execute, interpret, or critique—not merely recall a formula.

section: Now you try: rapid method map

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Final checklist

Define symbols and retain units.
Show the formula or Excel method used.
Check assumptions before interpreting output.
Use the correct tail, denominator, or base category.
Distinguish sample evidence from population claims.
Avoid causal wording without a causal design.
State limitations and answer the business question.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Closing reflection
Can you move independently through:
business question → method → Excel → validation → conclusion → limitation → recommendation?
That complete reasoning chain—not an isolated calculation—is the central skill of Business Statistics.

Why test a hypothesis?
A sample estimate rarely equals a stated benchmark exactly. A test asks whether the difference is too large to explain readily by sampling variation, assuming the benchmark is true.

The null hypothesis states the benchmark.
The alternative hypothesis states the direction of evidence sought.
The significance level \alpha is the preselected threshold for a false rejection.
The p-value measures how extreme the observed statistic is under the null model.

section: Calculate the statistic from raw observations
text:
Calculate the statistic from raw observations
For n independent observations of one numerical outcome:
\bar x=\text{sample mean},\qquad
SE=\frac{s}{\sqrt n},\qquad
t=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{SE},\qquad df=n-1.
In Excel use COUNT, AVERAGE and STDEV.S for the sample summaries, then calculate SE and t in labelled cells. For a right-sided test, the p-value is =T.DIST(-t_cell,df_cell,TRUE). The t distribution is symmetric, so this left-tail calculation equals the right-tail area without subtracting a number close to 1.

text:
What this test does not compare
A one-sample test compares one population mean with a fixed benchmark. It does not test whether two model or property-group means differ, even when both groups appear in a descriptive chart.
The benchmark and the chosen significance level should be set before inspecting the data. A statistically clear result still depends on the sampling design, measurement quality and whether the business benchmark is meaningful.

If p<\alpha, reject H_0 and describe the evidence for H_1. If p\ge\alpha, fail to reject H_0: the sample does not give sufficient evidence for H_1 at that threshold.
Failure to reject does not prove equality. The p-value does not measure the chance that the null is true.

Sampling and variation

Watch me: diagnose a survey / Now you try: redesign the evidence






SolutionSolution 1 






The app demonstration targets all relevant users, but the frame contains only active users who see the prompt. Inactive or departed users are missed, and “excellent” leads respondents toward a positive answer. Use neutral wording, a defined recent-user population, a sample drawn from the customer list, and follow-up for non-response. In the smartwatch exercise, selecting only customers who exercised yesterday excludes less active users; voluntary email response adds self-selection. A huge sample from that biased frame reduces random error but not selection or wording bias. Sample randomly from all purchasers in a defined period, measure baseline and later activity consistently, and compare with an appropriate control or before/after design. Generalise only to the population represented by the sampling frame, subject to non-response.






Watch me: compare sample sizes / Now you try: sampling variation






SolutionSolution 2 






With \(\sigma=20\), \(SE(\bar X)\) is 4 at \(n=25\) and 2 at \(n=100\). With \(\sigma=48\), it is 8 at \(n=36\) and 4 at \(n=144\). The larger sample gives a more precise mean estimate. Halving standard error requires four times the sample size because \(SE=\sigma/\sqrt n\). Neither calculation fixes non-response bias.

Now you try: scenario analysis






SolutionSolution 8 






At fixed estimate and sample size, 90% gives the narrowest interval, then 95%, then 99%. At fixed variability, increasing \(n\) from 50 to 200 to 800 halves the standard error each time. For a mean, \(SE=s/\sqrt n\) (or \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) when known); for a proportion, \(SE=\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}\). A manager can plan for wider intervals at higher confidence and can quadruple a random sample to roughly halve margin of error; neither tactic repairs biased sampling.

title: Week 3 — instructor solutions
text:
Retrieval and closing checks
A parameter describes the population; a statistic is calculated from a sample. In \(P(A\mid B)\), the denominator is the number or probability in group \(B\). A \(t\) distribution accounts for uncertainty from estimating the population SD in mean inference. Large datasets can still miss part of the target population. Sampling variation shrinks as \(n\) grows; selection bias does not. The law of large numbers says averages stabilise toward a population mean under appropriate sampling, while the central limit theorem supports an approximately Normal sampling distribution of the mean under suitable conditions as \(n\) grows. Report interval bounds as evidence with assumptions, not certainty about a fixed parameter.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Probability turns a count into a chance
text:
Probability turns a count into a chance
ETF defines probability as a numerical value representing the chance, likelihood or possibility that an event will occur. It lies between 0 and 1.
An event is one or more outcomes of an experiment. A sample space S collects all possible simple outcomes. For one fair die roll, S={1,2,3,4,5,6} and P(S)=1.
A sample frequency can estimate a probability when the sample and observation process are suitable. Always name the population or process the estimate describes.

The addition rule removes the double-counted intersection:
P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).
If A and B cannot occur together, they are mutually exclusive and P(A\cap B)=0.

Intersection of two events from ETF’s probability lecture.The shaded overlap is A\cap B. When adding P(A) and P(B), that region is included twice, so the union formula subtracts it once.

text:
Mutually exclusive and independent
These are different ideas:

Mutually exclusive: the events cannot happen together.
Independent: knowing one occurred does not change the probability of the other.

If two nonzero-probability events are mutually exclusive, observing one rules out the other. They are therefore not independent. We test independence through conditional probabilities after building a table.

Joint and marginal probabilities
A joint probability describes a pair of categories, the intersecting cell divided by the grand total. A marginal probability describes one variable, the relevant row or column total divided by the grand total.

text:
Conditional probability changes the denominator
ETF describes conditional probability as the probability of one event given information that another event has occurred:
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}
=\frac{\text{count of both A and B}}{\text{count of B}},\qquad P(B)>0.
The condition, after the vertical bar, defines the smaller group. P(A\mid B) generally differs from P(B\mid A).

Independence: compare conditional and marginal
Events A and B are independent if learning B does not change A’s probability:
P(A\mid B)=P(A), \quad\text{equivalently}\quad
P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B).

Standard Normal and Student’s t
A standard Normal has mean 0 and SD 1. Standardisation puts unlike measurements on a common scale:
z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}.
ETF introduces the t distribution because estimating an unknown population SD from a sample adds uncertainty. It resembles the standard Normal but has heavier tails for small degrees of freedom; as degrees of freedom grow, the two become close. Week 3 uses these critical values for intervals.

A precise Excel probability from an unsuitable model can be misleading.

3. Estimate uncertainty — 20 marks






SolutionSolution 5 






iPhone 4 issue-report proportion. There are \(x=11\) reports among \(n=2{,}000\) owners, giving \(\hat p=11/2000=0.0055\) or 0.55%. The ordinary large-sample interval used in Weeks 3–4 has
\[SE(\hat p)=\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}=0.001654,\]
\[\hat p\pm1.96SE=0.0055\pm0.003241=\boxed{[0.002259,\ 0.008741]},\]
or [0.226%, 0.874%]. The sample 3GS rate is \(8/2000=\mathbf{0.40\%}\), a descriptive comparison rather than a formal difference test. Under the stated random sampling from the fictional customer list and accurate record linkage, the procedure gives a 95% confidence interval for the population proportion of iPhone 4 purchasers who reported an issue in the prior 30 days. The success/failure counts are 11 and 1,989; the small success count makes the Normal approximation less robust than it would be for a common event. The interval concerns support reporting, not all reception problems.
iPhone 4 mean handset loss. With \(n=100\), \(\bar x=2.791\) dB and \(s=1.3126\) dB, \(SE=s/\sqrt n=0.13126\) dB. Using \(t_{0.975,99}=1.9842\) gives
\[2.791\pm1.9842(0.13126)=\boxed{[2.531,\ 3.051]\text{ dB}}.\]
This is a 95% interval for the mean loss among handsets in the fictional test population, assuming an appropriate random sample and a reasonable sampling distribution of the mean. It is not a range for 95% of individual handsets.
The stated sample sizes reduce random uncertainty, but they do not repair a narrow customer list, non-response, record errors, or lab conditions that differ from real use. The two datasets have different target populations and cannot be pooled into one interval.

Calculate the statistic at the null boundary \(\mu_0=3\) dB. This is a one-sample, right-sided t test of the iPhone 4 handset losses. From the 100 iPhone 4 losses, \(SE=s/\sqrt n=1.3126/\sqrt{100}=0.13126\) dB. The statistic is
\[t=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}
=\frac{2.791-3}{0.13126}

The right-tail p-value is =T.DIST(1.592293,99,TRUE), approximately 0.943. The t distribution is symmetric, so the left-tail area at \(-t\) equals the right-tail area at \(t\); the worksheet formula =T.DIST(-t_cell,df_cell,TRUE) works for either sign. Fail to reject \(H_0\) at 5%: this sample does not provide evidence that the iPhone 4 population mean reception loss exceeds 3 dB. It also does not prove that the population mean is at or below 3 dB.
The observed iPhone 4 mean is 0.209 dB below the threshold; a one-sided 95% lower confidence bound is about 2.573 dB. That lower bound does not establish that the mean exceeds 3 dB. The two-sided 95% interval in Part 3 includes 3 dB, showing why the observed sample mean alone is insufficient to settle whether the population mean is below the threshold. The observed 3GS mean is 2.584 dB and the descriptive sample mean gap is 0.207 dB, but this one-sample test gives no inferential conclusion about a difference between models. A Type I error would be concluding that the iPhone 4 population mean exceeds 3 dB when it is actually at or below 3 dB.

section: 5. Advise Corporate Affairs and PR — 15 marks
text:
5. Advise Corporate Affairs and PR — 15 marks






SolutionSolution 8 






The following sample recommendation uses two precise supported claims, includes contrary evidence, and identifies a claim to avoid.

We take the reception concern seriously and will publish the results of further testing. In our simulated survey, 6.0% of observed calls dropped among iPhone 4 purchasers, compared with 5.4% for iPhone 3GS purchasers. The new model did slightly worse on this observed customer measure. Support reports were uncommon—0.55% for iPhone 4 and 0.40% for iPhone 3GS—but a low support-contact rate does not mean calls did not drop. All-cause returns were 1.7% and 6.0%, respectively; the data do not identify which returns were due to reception. In separate handset tests, average reception loss was 2.79 dB for iPhone 4 and 2.58 dB for iPhone 3GS. Both sample means were below our 3 dB decision threshold. The one-sided test does not provide evidence that the iPhone 4 population mean exceeds 3 dB (p = 0.943), but it cannot prove that mean is below 3 dB. This test does not establish a difference between the models. The CEO should avoid claiming that iPhone 4 has no reception problem or that the lower return rate proves customers are satisfied. These samples cannot explain every dropped call or predict performance in all network conditions. We recommend publishing the methods, testing more handsets and real-world call conditions, and reporting results and corrective action promptly.

The CEO’s opening should acknowledge the concern before quoting reassuring figures. Any public version must make clear that this is a fictional teaching case, if shared outside the assignment context.

title: Individual written assignment
text:
The business case
You are a business analyst. Your company has launched iPhone 4, and reports of reception signals dropping are attracting growing public criticism. Customers noticed that when the iPhone was held in a specific way, the reception bars dropped off.
The CEO will address the media in 48 hours. The Corporate Affairs team has commissioned you to analyse the available evidence and develop a persuasive, statistically defensible narrative. Your findings will inform the CEO’s public statement. You must identify what the data demonstrate, what remains uncertain, and which claims the CEO can reasonably make.
The company wants to know whether the iPhone 4 experience differs from that of the previous iPhone 3GS. A low rate of complaints or returns might reassure customers, while a higher rate of dropped calls or greater reception loss might require a more careful response. A persuasive data story must account for all of these measures.
Use the assignment data workbook to prepare the briefing. The scenario is fictional; the workbook contains no actual company or historical customer data.

title: Individual written assignment
text:
Data and decision
The workbook has a READ ME sheet with a data dictionary and two independent datasets:

Customer survey: a simple random sample of 2,000 customers of each model from the company’s customer list, linked to support and returns records. Each row represents one customer. It records whether one observed call dropped, whether the purchaser reported a reception issue to customer support during the previous 30 days, and whether the phone was returned within 30 days for any reason. These are different events. Coverage and case use are also recorded.
Reception tests: a simple random sample of 100 distinct handsets of each model (iPhone 3GS and 4) tested under the same network conditions. Each handset has signal reading measured in decibel-milliwatts (dBm) when placed on a flat surface (ungripped) and held in a position as if making a call (gripped). Calculate reception loss = ungripped reading − gripped reading; a larger positive number means a greater loss.

The product team’s working rule is that an average reception loss greater than 3 dB for iPhone 4 handsets would be operationally important. This is the decision threshold for the test below. Reception loss is a difference between two dBm readings, so its unit is dB.
In the questions below, owner means an original customer, including someone who subsequently returned a phone. The survey deliberately samples the same number from each model.

title: Individual written assignment
text:
Your tasks

1. Describe the evidence (20 marks)

Identify the observational unit, population of interest, sample, and type of the main variables in each sheet. Explain why the survey and reception tests answer different questions.
Build a compact CEO evidence table by phone model. Show the sample size; the rates of dropped calls. Include appropriate description statistics of reception loss. Importantly, distinguish between


customers who only reported a reception issue in the last 30 days
customers who only returned the phone for any reason

Use clear denominators and units so the table could be understood in a media briefing.
Support your table with two well-labelled charts: one comparing a drop our rates by model and one showing the distribution of reception loss by model.

Explain which headline figures would best answer the public concern. Identify one possible source of sampling or measurement bias.



2. Probability and reported issues (20 marks)
Using the Customer survey sheet, construct a contingency table for model and call_dropped. Show counts and relevant proportions. Calculate and interpret, as sample-based probability estimates:

P(\text{call dropped}\mid\text{iPhone 4});
P(\text{iPhone 4 and call dropped});
P(\text{reported issue}\mid\text{call dropped}); and
P(\text{call dropped or reported issue}).

State the denominator for each calculation. Compare the conditional call-drop probabilities for the two models and explain why this comparison alone does not establish that the handset model caused the difference. You may use a pivot table or Excel formulas; show enough working to make the calculations auditable.


3. Estimate uncertainty (20 marks)

Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of iPhone 4 owners in the customer population who reported a reception issue in the previous 30 days. State the estimate, standard error, interval, assumptions, and interpretation. Compare the estimate descriptively with the iPhone 3GS sample proportion.
Calculate a 95% confidence interval for mean reception loss among iPhone 4 handsets in the fictional test population. State the estimate, standard error, interval, assumptions, and interpretation.
Explain how sample size and sampling design affect how much confidence Corporate Affairs should place in these intervals.



4. Test the mean reception-loss claim (25 marks)
Use the Reception tests sheet to test, at the 5% significance level, whether the fictional iPhone 4 population has a mean reception loss greater than the 3 dB decision threshold.

State the parameter, null and alternative hypotheses, and explain why a one-sample, one-sided test is appropriate.
Show the iPhone 4 sample size, mean, standard deviation, standard error, test statistic, degrees of freedom, and p-value. Make your calculations auditable in Excel.
Give a decision and a plain-language conclusion about the 3 dB threshold. Explain what the result does and does not say about the two phone models, and describe a Type I error in this setting.



5. Advise Corporate Affairs and PR (15 marks)
Write a 150–250 word media-briefing recommendation for the Corporate Affairs and PR team. Propose a clear opening message for the CEO and two precise claims that the simulated evidence supports. Bring together the descriptive, probability, interval, and test results, including any result that complicates a reassuring message. Identify one claim the CEO should avoid, explain what remains uncertain, and recommend a next investigation or communication step. The team will use this advice to address public concerns, so write for a non-technical audience without overstating what the data shows.

What is business statistics?
ETF defines business statistics as the application of statistical tools and methods to analyse data for evidence-based business decisions.
A business question comes first. For example: Do property prices differ between homes inside and outside a school zone? The answer needs a clear unit, a relevant population, useful measurements and a conclusion with limitations.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Variable, observation and data

A variable is a characteristic of an item or individual.
Data are the observed values of variables.
An observation is one item or individual measured.

In the RealEstate sheet of the Week 1 workbook, one row is one property. Price ($000s), Beds, SchoolZone and Auction are variables. A price of 1100 means AUD 1.1 million.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Population, sample, parameter, statistic

Population: all members of the group about which we want a conclusion.
Sample: a subset selected for analysis, ideally representative of that population.
Parameter: a numerical description of the population, usually unknown.
Statistic: a numerical description computed from the sample.

A mean calculated from 329 sampled properties is a statistic. It is evidence about a population mean only if the sample and population are defined and the sampling process is credible.

section: One number cannot describe a distribution
text:
One number cannot describe a distribution
Numerical description has three parts:

Centre: mean and median describe a typical value.
Spread: standard deviation and IQR describe variability.
Shape: symmetry, skewness and unusual values affect interpretation.

ETF Seminar Week 4 uses all three when comparing house prices by school zone. A chart shows features a single average can hide.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Mean, median and mode

Mean: sum of observations divided by their number, =AVERAGE(range). It uses every value and is affected by extreme prices.
Median: the middle ordered value, =MEDIAN(range). Half the values are at or below it.
Mode: the most frequent value, =MODE.SNGL(range). For prices with few repeats, a modal interval in a histogram is often more useful.

If a few very expensive houses pull the mean above the median, describe the distribution as right-skewed before choosing the headline statistic.

The sample standard deviation measures how observations vary around the sample mean: =STDEV.S(range). It uses all values but responds to outliers.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Today’s question
What can one sample tell us about a population, and how uncertain is that estimate?
The lecture follows the ETF sequence: sampling design → sampling distribution → standard error → confidence interval. We apply the same logic to a mean and a proportion.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
The direction of inference
A population contains the units about which we want a conclusion. We observe a sample, compute a statistic, and use it to estimate a population parameter.



Population parameter
Sample statistic




Mean \mu
Mean \bar x


Standard deviation \sigma
Standard deviation s


Proportion \pi
Proportion \hat p=x/n



A number in Excel is a sample statistic until the population and sampling method justify a broader claim.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Why sample selection matters
ETF’s simple random sample gives each population member an equal chance of selection. The goal is to reduce bias, systematic favouring of some outcomes.
An in-app food-delivery poll misses nonusers. A train survey only at 8–9 am Friday may miss other travellers. A large sample from the wrong frame can still give an invalid population conclusion.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Watch me: diagnose a sample
A customer-list survey estimates a population defined by the list. Check:

Who is in the target population?
Who could actually be selected?
How were units selected?
Who did not respond or was not measured?
Could the recorded variable differ from the intended one?

This check belongs beside every interval, because a narrow numerical interval cannot repair selection or measurement bias.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
The sampling distribution
ETF defines the sampling distribution of \bar x as the distribution of all possible sample means from all possible samples of a fixed size n.
We observe only one mean, but another random sample would usually give another value. Across repeated samples, the mean of \bar x is the population mean \mu; the SD of \bar x is the standard error:
SE(\bar x)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
This is a statement about variation between sample means, not variation between individual observations.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Shape and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
Shape and the Central Limit Theorem
If the population is Normal, the sample mean is Normal for any sample size. For a sufficiently large independent sample, the Central Limit Theorem makes the distribution of \bar x approximately Normal even when the individual data are not Normal.
ETF uses n\ge 30 as a useful classroom guide, with a separate check for severe skewness or outliers. Larger n reduces SE because of the square root in the denominator.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Point estimate plus margin of error
text:
Point estimate plus margin of error
ETF calls the observed \bar x a point estimate. Because it varies from sample to sample, report a range of plausible values for \mu:
\text{confidence interval}=\text{estimate}\ \pm\ \text{critical value}\times SE.
The confidence level describes the long-run success of this sampling-and-interval procedure. For 95% confidence, 2.5% of the reference distribution lies in each tail.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
The middle 95%

ETF confidence-area diagram: the central 95 percent and two 2.5 percent tails.The diagram explains why Excel uses the 97.5th percentile for the upper critical value. The centre is the interval’s coverage target across repeated samples.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Known population SD: use z
When \sigma is genuinely known and the sampling conditions hold:
\bar x\pm z^*\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n},
\qquad z^*=\texttt{NORM.S.INV}(0.975)\approx1.960
\quad\text{for 95\% confidence.}
The units of the interval match the units of \bar x. The standard error becomes smaller as n grows.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Unknown population SD: use t
Usually \sigma is unknown, so ETF replaces it with the sample SD s and uses a t critical value with n-1 degrees of freedom:
\bar x\pm t^*_{n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt n},
\qquad t^*_{n-1}=\texttt{T.INV}(0.975,n-1).
In Excel, T.INV.2T(0.05,n-1) gives the same positive 95% critical value. The t distribution’s extra tail area reflects estimating the SD.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: A proportion estimates how common an event is
text:
A proportion estimates how common an event is
ETF uses \pi for a population proportion and \hat p=x/n for the sample proportion, where x is the count with a named characteristic.
For a shopper outcome, define both the event and the denominator. \hat p lies between 0 and 1. A sample proportion also varies across repeated samples.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
The proportion standard error
For a large enough sample, the distribution of \hat p is approximately Normal. For an interval, use the observed proportion in the estimated SE:
\widehat{SE}(\hat p)=
\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}.
ETF’s classroom check requires both n\hat p\ge5 and n(1-\hat p)\ge5. These are counts of observed successes and failures. A rare event near the threshold deserves a cautious interpretation.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
The 95% proportion interval
\hat p\pm z^*
\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}},
\qquad z^*=\texttt{NORM.S.INV}(0.975).
The result is a proportion. Multiply endpoints by 100 to report percentages, and use the same denominator in the estimate and standard error. This familiar interval is an approximation, especially for very rare outcomes.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Interpreting 95% confidence
A defensible conclusion says: “Using this sampling procedure, we are 95% confident that the population proportion [or mean] is between the two reported bounds.”
It does not assign 95% probability to a fixed parameter after the sample is observed. It does not make the sample representative. State sampling, independence, approximation and measurement limitations alongside the number.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics

Population and event → sampling design → count or mean from raw rows → standard error and conditions → critical value → interval → interpretation and limitation.

For the exercise: (1) \(H_0:\mu=30\), \(H_1:\mu>30\), right; (2) \(H_0:\mu=85\), \(H_1:\mu\ne85\), two-sided; (3) \(H_0:\pi=0.04\), \(H_1:\pi<0.04\), left; (4) \(H_0:\pi=0.50\), \(H_1:\pi>0.50\), right. Boundary wording such as “at least 98%” can be represented by a composite null \(\pi\ge0.98\); calculations use its boundary value.

Click-through: \(t=(10.8-12)/(3.2/\sqrt{45})=\mathbf{-2.516}\), \(df=44\), and =T.DIST(-2.515576,44,TRUE) gives 0.00780. At 5%, reject \(H_0\); the sample supports a mean below 12 clicks per minute, assuming the test conditions hold.

Reject at 5%; there is evidence that population mean monthly discretionary spending exceeds AUD 275. The estimated difference is AUD 8. A random sample is stated; the test also needs a sufficiently reasonable sampling distribution of the mean.

For all 329 properties, the sample mean price is 1,215.462 and sample SD is 418.922 in AUD thousands. Test \(H_0:\mu\le1200\) against \(H_1:\mu>1200\). The standard error is 23.0959, giving \(t=(1215.462-1200)/23.0959=\mathbf{0.6695}\) with \(df=328\). Excel’s =T.DIST(-0.669469,328,TRUE) gives 0.2518. At 5%, fail to reject: the sample does not give sufficient evidence that population mean price exceeds AUD 1.2 million. The sample mean alone being above the threshold is insufficient.
For the 67 properties with SchoolZone=No, the sample mean is 1,046.045 and SD is 361.761 in AUD thousands. Test \(H_0:\mu\le1000\) against \(H_1:\mu>1000\). The standard error is 44.1962, \(t=\mathbf{1.0418}\), \(df=66\), and =T.DIST(-1.041827,66,TRUE) gives 0.1506. Fail to reject at 5%. The inference applies only to a population that the selected properties could reasonably represent; filtering records does not itself create a random sample.

Proportion tests and interval

Watch me: transaction success rate / Now you try: invoice accuracy






SolutionSolution 5 






Bank: \(\hat p=229/250=0.916\). Under \(H_0:\pi=0.95\), expected successes and failures are 237.5 and 12.5, both at least 5. \(z=\mathbf{-2.467}\); =NORM.S.DIST(-2.466619,TRUE) gives 0.00682. Reject at 10%; there is evidence of a success rate below 95%.
Invoices: \(H_0:\pi=0.98\) (or \(\pi\ge0.98\)), \(H_1:\pi<0.98\). The audit gives \(\hat p=288/300=0.96\). Null expected successes/failures are 294 and 6; the slide’s threshold of 5 is met, but the smaller failure count makes the Normal approximation worth noting. \(z=(0.96-0.98)/\sqrt{0.98(0.02)/300}=\mathbf{-2.474}\); =NORM.S.DIST(-2.474358,TRUE) gives 0.00667. Reject at 5%; the data support an accuracy rate below 98% under the stated approximation.






Now you try: interval cross-check






SolutionSolution 6 






The ordinary 95% Wald interval uses the sample rate in its standard error: \(0.96\pm1.96\sqrt{0.96(0.04)/300}=\mathbf{[93.78\%,98.22\%]}\). It includes 98%. This is consistent with a two-sided 5% test failing to reject, while the prespecified left-sided test rejects. The interval shows plausible effect sizes and uncertainty; do not claim it contradicts the one-sided result.

title: Week 4 — instructor solutions
text:
Decisions, errors and importance

Watch me: errors in context / Now you try: business consequences






SolutionSolution 7 






For the spending claim, a Type I error means concluding mean spending exceeds AUD 275 when it does not; a Type II error means missing a true excess. For invoices, a Type I error is concluding accuracy is below 98% when it is at least 98%, potentially causing needless process changes and cost. A Type II error is failing to detect accuracy below 98%, leaving customers and staff exposed to errors. 5% is a defensible default; 10% may be chosen if missed errors are especially costly, while 1% reduces false alarms at the cost of less detection power. Choose \(\alpha\) before inspecting the sample and explain the relative costs; there is no universal correct level.






Now you try: challenge the headline






SolutionSolution 8 






\(p<0.001\) is evidence against a zero mean reduction under the test model. It does not establish a major improvement or that the redesign caused it. Report the 0.2-minute = 12-second estimate, a confidence interval, a pre-set meaningful threshold, baseline wait and implementation cost, and the study design. A defensible statement is: “The observed mean wait was 12 seconds lower with strong statistical evidence, but its operational value and causal attribution require further assessment.”

title: Week 4 — instructor solutions

Integrated evidence brief

Watch me: audit a testing worksheet / Now you try: complete the evidence brief






SolutionSolution 9 






A worked one-page option is to test whether more than half the target market has tried the product. From Marketing, 495 of 856 report trial, \(\hat p=0.57827\). State \(H_0:\pi=0.50\), \(H_1:\pi>0.50\), \(\alpha=0.05\). Null expected counts are 428 successes and 428 failures. \(z=(0.57827-0.50)/\sqrt{0.5(0.5)/856}=\mathbf{4.58}\); =1-NORM.S.DIST(4.58,TRUE) gives about 0.0000023. Reject \(H_0\); there is evidence that the population proportion is above half, conditional on representative sampling. The 95% interval is [54.52%, 61.14%]. A Type I error would be declaring majority trial when true trial is at most half. Recommendation: “Plan for a majority-tried segment, but validate the survey frame before applying this estimate to the full market. Track non-response and repeat with a probability sample if a high-cost launch decision depends on the precise proportion.”

A confidence interval estimates a population parameter with a method having a stated long-run coverage rate. A standard error measures sample-statistic variability across repeated samples. Choose the test tail from the claim before computing, and use “reject” or “fail to reject” with a contextual conclusion. A small p-value measures evidence under the null, not the size of a business benefit.

Covariance
Sample covariance measures joint movement:
s_{XY}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{n-1}.

Positive: variables tend to move in the same direction.
Negative: variables tend to move in opposite directions.
Magnitude depends on measurement units, limiting comparison.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Correlation
Correlation standardises covariance:
r=\frac{s_{XY}}{s_Xs_Y},\qquad -1\le r\le1.

Sign gives direction.
Magnitude gives strength of linear association.
Correlation is unit-free and symmetric in X and Y.

SolutionSolution 2

title: Week 8 — instructor solutions
text:
Relationships and service quality

Watch me: correlation matrix / Now you try: prioritise relationships






SolutionSolution 3 






Run Data > Data Analysis > Correlation on labelled numerical columns; the diagonal should be 1 and the matrix symmetric. Excluding the store ID, the strongest positive correlations with Profit are PedCount 0.450, MTenure 0.439, Pop 0.431; the strongest negative is Comp −0.335. For ServQual, MgrSkill 0.357 is strongest positive; CrewSkill is weak at −0.034. Plot Profit versus MTenure and Profit versus Comp (or PedCount), looking for unusual points and nonlinearity. Pop and PedCount correlate 0.608, a possible collinearity concern if both enter a model. A weak marginal relationship, such as Hours24 with Profit (\(r\approx-0.026\)), can still have a conditional coefficient when other store factors are held constant. Say “in these stores, higher manager tenure tends to accompany higher profit” and “more measured competition tends to accompany lower profit”; neither is a causal finding.






Now you try: compare service groups






SolutionSolution 4 






Create =IF(M2>=90,1,0) if ServQual is in M; 37 stores meet the threshold and 38 do not. MgrSkill mean is 3.782 for excellent-service stores versus 3.498 otherwise; medians 3.683 versus 3.472. CrewSkill means are 3.434 versus 3.479; medians 3.500 versus 3.425. Side-by-side boxplots and SDs (about 0.39 for manager skill and 0.41 for crew skill in both groups) show overlap. The manager-skill difference is descriptively more pronounced; this classification discards score information and does not establish a causal effect.






Watch me: service-quality model / Now you try: refine the service model






SolutionSolution 5 






With all four staffing predictors, ToolPak gives
\[\widehat{ServQual}=53.664+0.02281\,MTenure+0.01876\,CTenure+10.1462\,MgrSkill-1.3645\,CrewSkill.\]
At fixed other predictors, one additional manager-tenure month is associated with 0.0228 more predicted service-quality points; one manager-skill unit with 10.15 more. Adjusted \(R^2=\mathbf{0.0906}\), residual SE 12.03 points, Significance F 0.0303. Only MgrSkill has a clearly small individual p-value (0.0054); MTenure 0.376, CTenure 0.824, CrewSkill 0.703. A defensible focused reduction keeps MgrSkill alone:
\[\widehat{ServQual}=47.081+11.0152\,MgrSkill.\]
Its adjusted \(R^2\) is 0.1153, residual SE 11.86, overall p-value 0.00168, and MgrSkill p-value 0.00168. The coefficient is similar to the full model’s 10.15. The simpler model is preferable for an exploratory service-quality summary, while retaining the full model may be justified by a prior staffing theory. Inspect residuals for structure, unequal spread and ceiling effects near 100; both models explain little of the score variation.

title: Week 8 — instructor solutions
text:
Profit and decision

Watch me: profit model / Now you try: decision model






SolutionSolution 6 






A full contextual model with MTenure, CTenure, MgrSkill, CrewSkill, ServQual, Pop, Comp, Visibility, PedCount, Res, Hours24 has adjusted \(R^2=\mathbf{0.6637}\), residual SE AUD 51,849, and Significance F about \(2.77\times10^{-13}\). Res=1 denotes residential context and Hours24=1 denotes 24-hour operation; their zero categories are bases. In this model, the manager-tenure slope is AUD 684 per month (\(p<0.0001\)), crew-tenure AUD 870 per month (\(p=0.0335\)), and manager-skill AUD 45,197 per score unit (\(p=0.0090\)), all conditional on other included variables. CrewSkill and Visibility have large p-values; Pop and PedCount correlate, so check coefficient stability. Even a statistically clear effect may not cover the cost of an incentive.
A transparent reduced model removes CrewSkill, ServQual and Visibility while retaining tenure, manager skill and store-context controls:
\[\begin{aligned}
\widehat{Profit}={}&-131266.99+724.64\,MTenure+806.36\,CTenure\\
&+57347.80\,MgrSkill+3.2705\,Pop-29779.05\,Comp\\
&+31364.34\,PedCount+91706.36\,Res+65092.73\,Hours24.
\end{aligned}\]
For example, at fixed other predictors, another month of manager tenure corresponds to AUD 725 more predicted annual profit, another month of crew tenure to AUD 806 more, and a one-unit manager-skill increase to AUD 57,348 more. Res compares residential-context stores with the zero base, and Hours24 compares operating categories, conditional on controls. All retained slopes have two-sided p-values below 0.05. Adjusted \(R^2=\mathbf{0.6498}\), residual SE AUD 52,904, Significance F about \(5.06\times10^{-14}\). Compared with the full model, fit falls slightly but interpretation is simpler; this is an exploratory reduction, not proof that omitted factors are irrelevant. For Store 1, predicted profit is AUD 261,597 versus actual AUD 265,014, residual AUD 3,417. Inspect residuals and influence before using the model for operational decisions.






Now you try: executive recommendation






SolutionSolution 7 






A five-sentence example: “Pilot a manager-retention incentive in a limited group of comparable stores before any chain-wide decision. In the reduced observational model, an additional month of manager tenure is associated with about AUD 725 more annual store profit at fixed included factors, with strong coefficient evidence and adjusted \(R^2\) of 0.650. That estimated association should be compared with incentive cost and a pre-set minimum worthwhile profit gain. Existing stores may differ in ways the workbook does not measure, so the regression does not establish an incentive’s causal return. Compare pilot stores with a suitable control group, track tenure and net profit, and revisit the policy after a defined period.”

title: Week 8 — instructor solutions
text:
Misconception clinic and exam practice

Now you try: correct the conditional claim






SolutionSolution 9 






“Among app users in the sample, 70% are highly satisfied” is the claim supported by the given figure. To calculate \(P(App\mid Satisfied)\), obtain the number who are both app users and satisfied and the total number of satisfied customers, or the full 2×2 table. The denominator changes from all app users to all satisfied customers.






Now you try: repair the interval statement






SolutionSolution 10 






A correct contextual form is: “Using this sampling method, we are 95% confident that the population mean [named quantity and units] lies between [calculated bounds].” In repeated sampling, about 95% of such intervals capture the fixed mean. A confidence interval for the mean is about uncertainty in the population average; it is not a range containing 95% of individual customer values.






Now you try: repair the coefficient claim






SolutionSolution 11 






In the reduced profit model, the Hours24 coefficient AUD 65,093 compares predicted annual profit for a 24-hour store (1) with a non-24-hour store (0), holding the other included predictors fixed. The base category is non-24-hour operation. Store selection, location or other unmeasured factors could explain part of the difference, so this is not a causal estimate of extending hours. A numerical slope such as MgrSkill has no base category; it is per one score unit.






Now you try: repair the evidence claim






SolutionSolution 12 






Use a template: “The estimated effect is [estimate with units], with a [confidence level] interval of [lower, upper]. The test gives [p-value] under its assumptions. Our pre-set business threshold is [amount]; because the plausible gain is [above/below/straddles] that threshold, [decision].” If a statistically clear effect is too small to cover cost or meet the threshold, do not recommend rollout on significance alone. The p-value is not a probability that \(H_0\) is true.






Watch me: decode an exam question / Now you try: rapid method map






SolutionSolution 13 






The slides leave the eight mini-scenarios to the instructor, so there is no unique numerical answer key. A complete response to each scenario identifies: target parameter or objective; variable types; one matching method; a critical assumption or constraint; the Excel command or formula; and a conclusion in context. Useful mappings span (1) category percentage → count/PivotTable; (2) Normal individual probability → NORM.DIST; (3) mean interval with unknown SD → T.INV.2T; (4) proportion test → null-based z statistic and NORM.S.DIST; (5) categorical association → contingency table, expected counts and CHISQ.TEST after Week 5, with conditional rates for practical interpretation; (6) simple regression → ToolPak Regression, scatterplot and residuals; (7) multiple regression → ToolPak Regression with coefficient and F tests; (8) listed-price choice → ToolPak demand model plus formula table, whole-unit and capacity rules. For every case, report units and avoid causal or global-optimum claims unsupported by the design.
